prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

That dusty bubble gum, once ubiquitous as starlings, is no more, my love. Whistling dinosaurs now populate only animation studios, the furious actions of angels causing their breasts to flop out in mannerist frescos flake away as sleet holds us in its teeth. And the bus-station's old urinals go under the grindstone and the youthful spelunkers graduate into the wrinkle-causing sun. The sea seemingly a constant to the naked eye is one long goodbye, perpetually the tide recedes, beaches dotted with debris. Unto each is given a finite number of addresses, ditties to dart the heart to its moments of sorrow and swoon. The sword's hilt glints, the daffodils bow down, all is temporary as a perfect haircut, a kitten in the lap, yet sitting here with you, my darling, waiting for a tuna melt and side of slaw seems all eternity I'll ever need and all eternity needs of me.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: That, Whistling, And

outputs.L1: That dusty bubble gum, once as ubiquitous as starlings, is no more, my love. Whistling dinosaurs now inhabit only animation studios; the furious motions of angels, causing their breasts to spill from mannerist frescoes, flake away as sleet holds us in its teeth. And the bus station’s old urinals pass beneath the grindstone, while youthful spelunkers graduate into the wrinkle-making sun. The sea, seemingly constant to the naked eye, is one long goodbye: perpetually, the tide recedes, and the beaches are dotted with debris. Unto each of us is given a finite number of addresses, ditties that dart the heart toward its moments of sorrow and swoon. The sword’s hilt glints; the daffodils bow down. All is as temporary as a perfect haircut, a kitten in the lap—yet sitting here with you, my darling, waiting for a tuna melt and a side of slaw, seems all the eternity I will ever need, and all the eternity that needs anything of me.
outputs.L2:
That powdery stick of bubble gum that used to be everywhere, as common as starlings, has vanished, my love. Dinosaurs that whistle survive now only in animation houses. In mannerist frescoes, the frantic movements of angels make their breasts spill free, even as the paintings peel and crumble, while sleet grips us in its jaws. The old urinals at the bus station are being worn down and destroyed, and the young cave explorers pass on into the sun that brings wrinkles.

The sea, which appears unchanging to an unaided eye, is really an extended farewell: the tide is always pulling back, and the beaches are scattered with wreckage. Every person receives only a limited allotment of addresses, and a limited supply of little songs that send the heart toward its episodes of grief and rapture. The sword handle flashes; the daffodils bend. Everything passes—like an ideal haircut, like a kitten resting in your lap. Still, seated here beside you, my darling, waiting for a tuna melt with coleslaw on the side, feels like all the forever I will ever require, and all the forever that could ever require me.
outputs.L3:
The speaker reflects on the way familiar things gradually vanish, even when they once seemed permanent. Streets, buildings, customs, and everyday scenes that used to feel ordinary and dependable are changed or erased by time. What was once common becomes distant, remembered only in fragments. This awareness gives the reflection a quiet sadness: nothing remains exactly as it was, and even the most familiar parts of life are subject to disappearance.

Images of decay and transformation deepen this sense of impermanence. Nature changes with the seasons, art fades or is forgotten, youth passes into age, and public spaces are altered by new generations and new uses. These examples suggest that no part of human experience is truly fixed. Beauty, vitality, and shared places may seem lasting in the moment, but they too are temporary. Everything is touched by time, whether slowly or suddenly.

The sea offers a powerful symbol in this meditation. At first, it appears constant, stretching endlessly and returning again and again with its waves. Yet the sea also represents departure, distance, and loss. It carries things away, separates people and places, and reminds the speaker that movement is continuous. Even what seems eternal is part of an ongoing process of change.

The speaker also recognizes that each life is limited. Every person is given only a finite number of places to know, songs to hear, and emotional moments to experience. There are only so many meetings, journeys, conversations, and memories that can belong to one lifetime. This realization makes ordinary experiences feel precious, because they cannot be repeated endlessly.

And yet, despite this universal impermanence, the speaker finds meaning in a simple moment shared with a loved one. In that moment, nothing grand or permanent is required. The presence of the beloved makes the experience feel whole. Though time will continue to pass and all things will change, the ordinary scene becomes complete, almost eternal, because it is filled with love and attention. The moment may not last forever in the world, but it feels timeless in the heart.
outputs.L4:
Everything is passing away, though not always with the drama we expect. More often, things vanish quietly: a chair left too long in the rain, a photograph fading at the edges, a toy buried under dust in an attic, a name no one says anymore. The world is full of these small disappearances. Cups crack, letters yellow, gardens go wild, houses lose their voices when the people who filled them are gone. Even the objects that once seemed solid and permanent become strange with time, as if they belonged to someone else’s dream.

Memory preserves them imperfectly. It does not return the past whole, but in fragments: the smell of old wood, the sound of a screen door closing, the pale shine of a vanished sea, the feel of a hand once held and then lost. In memory, ordinary things become surreal. A rusted bicycle may appear beside a field of snow. A childhood room may float like a boat in darkness. The faces of the dead may seem younger than our own. We carry these images with us, not as proof that anything can be saved, but as evidence that what disappears still leaves a shape behind.

Bodies, too, obey this law of change. Skin loosens, hair thins, breath grows shorter, and the mirror gradually becomes less familiar. The body that once ran without thinking begins to negotiate with stairs, cold mornings, and pain. Yet aging is not only decline; it is also a record. Every line and scar marks contact with the world. The body decays because it has lived, because it has touched, endured, desired, suffered, and loved. Its fragility is not separate from its meaning.

Places change in the same way. Streets are renamed, storefronts close, rivers shift their courses, and the sea withdraws from shores where it once seemed endless. Cliffs crumble grain by grain. Villages empty out. The landscapes we trusted as fixed are also moving, though sometimes too slowly for us to notice. A beach remembered from childhood may no longer exist; a tree that shaded generations may be gone by morning. Even the earth is not a monument. It is a process.

Against this immense fading, human life can seem unbearably brief. We build, collect, promise, and remember, but time loosens every knot. The things we love are already changing as we love them. Every embrace contains the knowledge of separation. Every home is temporary. Every season, even while it is blooming, is preparing to end.

And yet there are moments when this truth does not feel like defeat. Two people sit together at a table. Light falls across the room. Perhaps there is bread, a cup of tea, the sound of rain, the faint noise of traffic outside. Nothing extraordinary happens. No great revelation arrives. One person looks at the other and feels, for an instant, that nothing more is needed.

Such a moment does not stop time, but it changes our relation to it. Love does not make the world permanent. It does not keep the body young, restore the dead, or command the sea to return. But it gives fullness to what is brief. It allows an ordinary hour to feel complete in itself, not because it will last forever, but because it is wholly inhabited. In intimacy, the passing moment becomes enough.

This is the strange consolation at the heart of transience: everything is vanishing, and still the present can be abundant. The cracked cup, the aging hand, the fading photograph, the eroding coast—all belong to a world that cannot be held. But when love is shared, even simply and silently, the fragile world becomes sufficient. For a little while, within change and loss, we touch something that feels eternal.
outputs.L5:
That whistling sound came from the edge of the forest, soft at first and then clearer as the wind moved through the trees. It was not the song of a bird, and it was not the cry of any animal I knew. It rose and fell like a forgotten melody, pulling my attention away from the path ahead.

I stopped and listened.

The evening was quiet, and the sky had begun to turn gold behind the hills. Every leaf seemed still, yet the whistling continued. There was something strange about it, something both comforting and mysterious. That sound felt as if it belonged to a memory I had never lived.

And then, just as suddenly as it had started, the whistling faded.

I stood there for a moment longer, unsure whether to follow it or turn back. In the end, I smiled and continued down the path, carrying that small mystery with me into the fading light.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal, maximalist prose poem addressed to “my love” about impermanence, nostalgia, and finding eternity in a mundane diner lunch.
counterfactuals.output:
My love, the vinyl booth is cracked like an old prophecy, and the waitress wipes the table in slow lunar circles, erasing our fingerprints, our crumbs, the little continents of salt we made while talking about nothing—weather, errands, the broken hinge on the back door—nothing, which is the holiest subject, because it is where the universe hides when it wants to be held.

Outside, noon leans its yellow forehead against the window. Cars pass with their brief metallic souls. A man in a seed-company cap stirs his coffee as if summoning a drowned town from the bottom of the cup. The jukebox, unplugged for years, remembers every song ever wasted on the young. And you sit across from me with ketchup on your thumb, mortal and radiant, tearing open a packet of sugar like a tiny white letter from a country that has already vanished.

How many lunches have we lost, my love? How many sandwiches dissolved into blood and errands, how many bowls of soup rose as steam and became weather over cities we will never visit? Childhood calls from the pay phone near the bathrooms, though the receiver is only a black seashell full of static. It says: come back, come back, the afternoons are endless and your mother is still hanging towels in the sun, your father is still whistling somewhere beyond the garage, the dog is not yet buried beneath the lilacs. But the line goes dead before I can answer, and the waitress arrives with our plates, balancing heaven on her forearms.

Here is your grilled cheese, cut diagonally: two golden doors to the temple of hunger. Here are my fries, each one a small, salty comet, doomed and magnificent. Here is the pickle spear, green canoe of all summers. Here is the tomato soup, red planet with a skin of cooling gloss, and in its trembling surface I see empires collapsing, birthdays flickering out, the hair at our temples silvering like frost on the fields of old kingdoms. I see every room we have left behind still lit without us. I see our younger selves in borrowed jackets, walking away from the station in the rain, believing time was a road and not a mouth.

And yet, my love, dip the sandwich.

Watch how the bread enters the soup and returns changed.

This is the whole scripture: immersion, softening, disappearance, sweetness of ruin. The cheese stretches between your hand and the plate like a strand of molten afternoon, like the last gold thread tying the sun to the world. You laugh because it refuses to break. For one second, it is longer than history. For one second, it holds.

I want to live there—in the elastic yellow eternity between the bite and the bitten, in the fluorescent hum above us, in the clatter from the kitchen where pans ring like minor planets striking God’s pocket change. I want to live in the steam lifting from your coffee, in the blue bruise of your shadow on the laminate, in the way you say, pass the napkins, as if napkins were not the fragile flags of every surrender, as if passing them were not a vow made against oblivion.

Everything leaves, yes. The ice thins itself into water. The water remembers being cloud. The cloud forgets. Our bodies are brief diners on the highway of the stars, open all night, closing soon. Even the mountains are only slow bread, being eaten by rain. Even the moon is a plate someone keeps clearing and returning, clearing and returning, until the hunger of darkness is satisfied.

But today, my love, eternity wears a paper hat in the kitchen. Eternity refills our coffee without being asked. Eternity is the chipped mug warming your palms, the chrome napkin dispenser reflecting us into a thousand bent and shining ghosts, the check face-down between us like a verdict or a love note. Eternity is not elsewhere. It is not beyond the blue exit sign, not after the final breath, not hidden in the cathedral vaults of galaxies. It is here, under the buzzing light, where you are licking salt from your finger, where I am pretending not to memorize you and failing, where the ordinary opens its greasy, tender mouth and sings.

So let the clock above the counter shed its minutes like scales. Let the booths empty. Let the waitress grow wings of receipt paper and fly backward into her childhood. Let the jukebox bloom with extinct music. Let every lunch we ever ate return as a flock of bright plates circling overhead. Let nostalgia be not a wound but a window we can fog with our breathing. Let impermanence be not theft but choreography: the hand reaching, the soup cooling, the cheese breaking at last, the two of us laughing as it falls.

My love, when we are gone—and we will go, we will go like steam from soup, like sugar into coffee, like the last neon letter burning out above a road nobody takes anymore—may some impossible future lean close to this booth and hear, beneath the crumbs, beneath the vinyl, beneath the faint cathedral of the lunch rush, the small forever we made here:

two spoons,

one check,

your knee touching mine under the table,

and the whole vanishing world unable to vanish.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a single-paragraph lyrical meditation in the style of contemporary American prose poetry, mixing absurd images, decay, romance, and ending with waiting for a tuna melt and slaw.
counterfactuals.output: The moon had the manners of a vending machine, blinking its small refusals over the parking lot where weeds came up through the asphalt like green rumors from a buried empire, and you stood beside me in your thrift-store coat, smelling faintly of rain and oranges, while the dumpsters dreamed their blue metallic dreams and a raccoon, priest of all leftover things, lifted its mask toward the ruined stars. I wanted to tell you love is not a rose but the mold blooming on the rose’s forgotten water, not the song but the cracked speaker humming after the party, not forever but the beautiful, stupid persistence of a plastic flamingo leaning into winter. Around us, the city softened and spoiled: brick turned to dust, pigeons argued over a French fry like philosophers over God, a billboard peeled its own face off in strips, and still your hand found mine with the tenderness of a match lit inside a refrigerator. Somewhere a siren practiced grief; somewhere a bride threw her bouquet into an open grave; somewhere the ocean was learning to impersonate a telephone. We laughed because the world was ending in coupons and thunder, because our hearts were two dented cans rolling toward the same gutter, because even ruin has a pulse if you press your ear to it long enough, and there we were, radiant with hunger, waiting for a tuna melt and slaw.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me an ornate, melancholic love letter that starts with vanished childhood candy and moves through strange apocalyptic imagery before resolving in a tender everyday moment.
counterfactuals.output:
Do you remember those vanished childhood candies—the ones that tasted less like sugar than like a small, impossible country we were allowed to visit for the length of an afternoon? I mean the chalky moons, the wax-bottled syrups, the violet lozenges wrapped in paper thin as moth wings; all those bright little relics that disappeared from corner shops as quietly as grandparents leaving a room.

Sometimes I think my love for you began there, in the ache of wanting what had already gone: a flavor receding from the tongue, a bell above a shop door still trembling though no one stood beneath it, the gold dust of a summer evening caught in the sticky seams of a child’s palm. Even before I knew you, I was practicing your absence.

And then came the stranger seasons.

The sky learned to bruise without healing. Birds wrote frantic scripture over the roofs and vanished into a west so red it looked rehearsed. In dreams, the oceans climbed the stairwells wearing crowns of foam; clocks shed their hands like dead leaves; statues stepped down from their plinths and wandered the avenues, blind with rain. Once, I imagined the moon cracked open like an egg above the city, spilling pale fire into the gutters, while the stars went out one by one with the soft obedience of candles in a chapel no one visited anymore.

Through all of it—through sirens blooming at dawn, through gardens growing teeth, through the news speaking in the voice of an old iron gate—you remained the one human sentence I could still understand. If the horizon darkened, I looked for your lamp. If the world became a cathedral of ash, I searched for the print of your hand in the dust. If angels, ragged and fevered, crowded the intersections to sell prophecies from their pockets, I would have traded every revelation for the smallest certainty of you: your coat on the back of a chair, your hairpin on the sink, your sleep-warm voice saying my name as though names were not fragile things.

I have loved you not as heroes love in painted epics, all banners and trumpets and celestial permissions, but as the last match loves its box; as a shore loves the returning wreckage; as a house, long abandoned, loves the first footstep that proves it has not been forgotten.

Tonight, however, the apocalypse has mislaid our address.

The dishes are drying in their crooked little kingdom beside the sink. A spoon rests in a bowl with the grave dignity of a fallen sword. You are standing in the kitchen in your socks, frowning at the kettle as if it has personally betrayed you by taking so long to boil. Outside, rain moves gently over the windows, not as omen, not as punishment, but simply as weather. The world, for once, is only itself.

You turn and ask whether I want honey in my tea.

And beloved—after all the extinct candies of childhood, after the black suns and the flooded boulevards, after every trembling vision of endings—I find that this is the sweetness I had been mourning before I knew its name: your hand reaching into the cupboard, the small clink of cups, the ordinary mercy of being asked, the unbearable tenderness of answering yes.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dense, associative paragraph about transience where everything from bubble gum to dinosaurs, angels, urinals, beaches, haircuts, and kittens becomes a symbol of mortality.
counterfactuals.output: Bubble gum swells bright and ridiculous against the tongue, a pink planet doomed by its own thin skin, bursting into sweetness that hardens to a gray fossil under the desk; dinosaurs, too, were only larger chewers of time, leaving bones like punctuation marks in the sediment; angels molt invisibly in church ceilings, their feathers yellowing into dust; urinals receive the body’s brief chemistry and rinse it away with ceremonial indifference; beaches spend themselves grain by grain, each wave erasing the signature it has just written; haircuts fall in soft little funerals around the chair, proof that even identity must be swept up after closing; kittens, all pulse and milk and impossible softness, carry inside them the old clock of claws, sleep, hunger, and disappearance. Everything is practicing how to vanish: sugar losing flavor, marble losing shine, empires losing names, the mirror losing the face it was trusted to keep.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a weird poetic monologue to a darling companion, full of unexpected metaphors and surreal juxtapositions, concluding that sitting together in a diner is enough eternity.
counterfactuals.output:
Darling,

you arrive like a spoon bent by moonlight,  
like a telegram delivered to a cabbage,  
like a small brass band hiding in the lungs of a sleeping whale.  
I have tried to explain you to the furniture,  
but the chairs only blush and drag their wooden feet.

When you look at me, the clocks forget their legal names.  
The ceiling becomes a soft aquarium of unspoken weather.  
My heart—poor bureaucratic onion—  
stamps every feeling APPROVED, APPROVED, APPROVED  
until the ink runs purple down my ribs.

I have carried whole cities in my pockets for you:  
a rainy Paris made of lint,  
a New York balanced on the head of a match,  
a desert where each grain of sand sings a different national anthem.  
None of them were large enough.  
None of them had your elbow beside mine  
on a cracked vinyl booth.

Darling companion, my strange little lighthouse with knees,  
let us not chase the grand cathedral of forever.  
Let forever chase us, panting,  
through the revolving door,  
past the pie case where lemon meringue dreams of becoming a cloud,  
past the waitress with thunder in her pencil,  
past the coffee black as a priest’s old shoe.

Here, the ketchup bottle glows like a minor planet.  
Here, the forks lie down like silver insects.  
Here, our two mugs steam their ghostly speeches  
into the fluorescent republic of 2 a.m.

And if the universe must end,  
let it end politely,  
with a bell over the door  
and one last refill.

Because your hand near mine on this sticky table,  
your laugh folding itself into the napkins,  
the jukebox coughing up a song from the underworld—  
this is sufficient.  
This is the long corridor of stars in miniature.  
This is the afterlife wearing a paper hat.

Darling, sitting together in a diner  
is enough eternity.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
